original_question: For every achievable Cantor set C, do there exist achievable Cantorvals D' and D'' such that C + D' is a Cantorval while C + D'' is an interval?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 11 ("Algebraic sums and decompositions of achievement sets")
correct_elements: Your draft matches the paper's Problem 11 almost verbatim. It gets the right source class (achievable Cantor sets), the right existential quantifier pattern (for each such C, ask for two possibly different witnesses), the right witness class (achievable Cantorvals), the right operation (set sum), and the two intended output topological types (Cantorval and interval).
missing_details: The ambient setting is one-dimensional: all sets are subsets of R.
"Achievable" should be defined: a set is achievable if it is an achievement set E(x_n) of some absolutely convergent real series, i.e. E(x_n) = {sum_{n in A} x_n : A subset of N}.
The quantifier order should be explicit: for every achievable Cantor set C, there exist achievable Cantorvals D' and D'' (depending on C).
The operator + should be identified as the algebraic/Minkowski sum: A + B = {a+b : a in A, b in B}.
"Cantor set" means homeomorphic to the classical ternary Cantor set.
"Cantorval" should be understood in the paper's standard sense: a compact subset of R whose gap endpoints are accumulation points of both other gaps and nontrivial interval components.
"Interval" is an interval subset of R; in this compact-setting context it is automatically a compact interval.
No extra restrictions such as multigeometricity, centrality, equal fundamental interval, positivity of terms, or fixed Hausdorff dimension are part of this problem.
refined_question: Let C ⊂ R be an achievable Cantor set, i.e. C = E(x_n) = {∑_{n∈A} x_n : A ⊂ N} for some absolutely convergent real series ∑ x_n, and assume that C is homeomorphic to the classical ternary Cantor set. Must there exist achievable Cantorvals D', D'' ⊂ R such that, for the algebraic sum A+B := {a+b : a∈A, b∈B}, the set C + D' is a Cantorval and the set C + D'' is an interval?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 3 on algebraic sums. The exact nearest official formulation is Problem 11, which asks precisely whether every achievable Cantor set can be summed with one achievable Cantorval to obtain a Cantorval and with another achievable Cantorval to obtain an interval. The immediate context confirms this reading: Theorem 9 shows that sums of multiple copies of a single achievable Cantor set can pass from Cantor set to Cantorval to interval, and Theorem 10 gives the reverse-direction analogue starting from an achievable Cantorval and adding achievable Cantor sets. The paper's general definitions of achievement set, Cantor set, and Cantorval are given at the start of Section 1 and are the missing self-contained ingredients needed to make your draft fully stand-alone and paper-faithful.
